1.title: Start at the top-right corner
1.explanation: Set `i` to the first row and `j` to the last column. Each comparison at `A[i][j]` can eliminate a whole row or column; return immediately on equality.

1.title: Discard one row or column
1.explanation: A value larger than `B` eliminates the current column, so move left. A smaller value eliminates the current row, so move down; falling out of bounds means the target is absent.

2.title: Handle the empty-input base case
2.explanation: Keep the required method signature and return `0` only when both arrays are empty. The remaining cases are handled before partition search.

2.title: Resolve one-array medians
2.explanation: `singleAr` returns the middle item for odd length and averages the two middle items for even length. Use it when either input array is empty.

2.title: Search only the shorter array
2.explanation: Swap the arrays when needed so binary search runs on the shorter one. `half` is the required size of the combined left partition.

2.title: Materialize the four partition borders
2.explanation: Use negative and positive infinity when a partition side is empty. These sentinels let the same validity test cover boundary partitions without special branches.

2.title: Validate or move the partition
2.explanation: The partition is correct when both left borders are no larger than the opposite right borders. Otherwise move left when `Aleft` is too large, or right when it is too small.

3.title: Define the row-count search
3.explanation: The solution will binary-search a value, so it first defines `findCount(row, num)` to count how many items in one sorted row are `<= num`.

3.title: Count values at or below a candidate
3.explanation: Binary-search the final index whose value is `<= num`; returning `ans + 1` converts that index into a count.

3.title: Set the global value range
3.explanation: Take the smallest first element and largest last element across rows as the search bounds. The median rank is half the total element count.

3.title: Binary-search the matrix median
3.explanation: Sum `findCount(row, mid)` over all rows. If at most half the matrix is `<= mid`, move right; otherwise record `mid` and look for a smaller valid value.

4.title: Handle tiny values and open the search
4.explanation: Return directly for `0` and `1`, special-case `2`, then binary-search candidate roots from `0` through `A`.

4.title: Keep the largest safe candidate
4.explanation: Compare with `A / mid` instead of `mid * mid` to avoid multiplication overflow. When `mid` fits, save it and search higher; otherwise search lower.

5.title: Locate the rotation pivot
5.explanation: Binary-search for the peak where `A[mid]` exceeds both neighbors. The side whose ordering is broken tells the search which half still contains the pivot.

5.title: Define bounded binary search
5.explanation: Search a supplied inclusive range and return the matching index. This helper is reused for each sorted half of the rotated array.

5.title: Narrow the selected sorted half
5.explanation: Move `lo` right when the midpoint is smaller than the target, otherwise move `hi` left. Return `-1` when that half contains no match.

5.title: Search both sides of the pivot
5.explanation: Find the pivot, then binary-search `[0, pivot]` and `[pivot + 1, n - 1]`. Returning the first non-`-1` result restores the original array index.

5.title: Return the surviving match
5.explanation: Prefer the left-half result when it exists; otherwise return the right-half result, which is already `-1` if the target is absent.

6.title: Test one window length
6.explanation: `findSums` builds the sum of the first `k` elements. If that window already exceeds `B`, length `k` is infeasible.

6.title: Slide the fixed-size window
6.explanation: For each next position, subtract the element leaving the window and add the element entering it. Reject as soon as any length-`k` window exceeds `B`.

6.title: Binary-search the maximum length
6.explanation: Search lengths from `1` to `len(A)`. A feasible midpoint is saved and pushes `lo` right because every smaller length is also feasible.

6.title: Shrink after an infeasible midpoint
6.explanation: When any window violates the sum limit, move `hi` left. `ans` retains the largest feasible length found so far.

7.title: Build the arithmetic helpers
7.explanation: Euclid's algorithm computes `gcd`; `lcm(a, b)` uses division before multiplication. A candidate `x` contains `x/B + x/C - x/lcm` magical numbers.

7.title: Open binary search on the answer
7.explanation: Search the numeric range and evaluate how many magical numbers are `<= mid`. Equality records a candidate and continues left to find the A-th number itself.

7.title: Move by the candidate count
7.explanation: Too few magical numbers means `mid` is too small, so move right; too many means move left. Return the smallest recorded candidate modulo the required constant.

8.title: Reject impossible student counts
8.explanation: Every student needs at least one book, so fewer books than students has no valid allocation and returns `-1`.

8.title: Greedily test a page cap
8.explanation: Accumulate consecutive books for the current student. When the next book would exceed `pages`, start a new student with that book.

8.title: Set the answer-search bounds
8.explanation: More than `B` students makes a cap infeasible. Search from the largest single book to the sum of all books, because the answer cannot lie outside that range.

8.title: Minimize the feasible cap
8.explanation: A feasible midpoint becomes the current answer and moves `hi` left. An infeasible midpoint moves `lo` right because a larger page cap is required.

9.title: Count packets of one size
9.explanation: For a proposed packet size `k`, sum `people // k` across cities. The size works when that count can feed at least `B` people.

9.title: Search possible packet sizes
9.explanation: Packet size starts at `1` and cannot exceed the smallest city supply. Binary search this monotonic feasibility range.

9.title: Maximize the feasible size
9.explanation: When `mid` feeds everyone, save it and search larger sizes. Otherwise search smaller sizes; `ans` is the largest working packet size.

10.title: Initialize three sorted-array pointers
10.explanation: Start one pointer in each array and continue while all three remain valid. The current range is `max(A[i], B[j], C[k]) - min(...)`.

10.title: Advance the current minimum
10.explanation: Only moving the smallest current value can reduce the range; moving either other pointer cannot improve the present maximum-minus-minimum gap.

11.title: Measure the current triple
11.explanation: With one pointer per sorted array, compute the minimum and maximum selected values and update the smallest absolute spread seen.

11.title: Move the limiting pointer
11.explanation: Advance whichever array supplies the current minimum. This is the only move that can produce a tighter spread before one array is exhausted.

12.title: Count the three colors
12.explanation: Traverse the array once and count how many `0`, `1`, and `2` values occur as red, white, and blue.

12.title: Overwrite in sorted color order
12.explanation: Walk the indices again, writing all remaining red values first and then white values while decrementing their counts.

12.title: Fill the remaining positions with blue
12.explanation: Once red and white are exhausted, every remaining slot must be `2`. Return the same rewritten array.

13.title: Start from opposite ends
13.explanation: Use the smallest element of `A` and largest element of `B`. Their sum can then be adjusted monotonically toward `C`.

13.title: Apply distance and tie-breaking
13.explanation: Replace the answer on a smaller absolute difference. On a tie, prefer the smaller `A` index, then the smaller `B` index exactly as required.

13.title: Move the sum toward the target
13.explanation: If the sum is at least `C`, decrease `j`; otherwise increase `i`. Convert the saved indices back to their array values at the end.

14.title: Sort and fix the first number
14.explanation: After sorting, fix `A[i]` and use two pointers `j` and `k` for the remaining pair. Track the closest sum and its distance from `B`.

14.title: Capture improvements and exact matches
14.explanation: A smaller absolute difference replaces `ans`. If the sum equals `B`, it is optimal and can be returned immediately.

14.title: Steer the two-pointer sum
14.explanation: A sum above `B` is reduced by moving `k` left; a smaller sum is increased by moving `j` right. Return the best recorded sum after all triples.

15.title: Sort side lengths and open two pointers
15.explanation: For sorted side lengths, test the product `A[i] * A[j]` using one pointer at each end.

15.title: Count an entire valid band
15.explanation: When the product is below `B`, every partner from `i` through `j` works with `A[i]`; count both orientations and the square pair. Otherwise lower `j`.

16.title: Track seen indices and best distance
16.explanation: Map each value to an index and initialize the answer to infinity. Each repeat can then be compared with the stored occurrence in O(1).

16.title: Update on repeats
16.explanation: Save the first occurrence, and on repeats minimize the index gap. This source code never refreshes the stored index, which is why it can miss the nearest repeated pair.

17.title: Build prefix sums
17.explanation: Create cumulative sums so equal prefix values identify a zero-sum slice between their indices.

17.title: Record first and last occurrence
17.explanation: For each prefix value, keep its earliest and latest indices. Their separation is the longest zero-sum slice associated with that value.

17.title: Choose the longest equal-prefix span
17.explanation: Compare every stored index pair, preferring a longer span and then the earlier start on ties.

17.title: Also handle prefixes that are zero
17.explanation: A zero prefix means the slice starts at array index `0`. Compare those candidates, then translate saved prefix boundaries into the returned array slice.

18.title: Build the first frequency window
18.explanation: Count the first `B` elements and store its distinct count as the first result. A frequency map supports constant-time additions and removals.

18.title: Remove the outgoing value
18.explanation: For each shift, decrement `A[i-B]`; when its count reaches zero, the window has lost one distinct value.

18.title: Add the incoming value
18.explanation: Create a missing key with zero count, increase the distinct total when that count was zero, then increment it and append the new window result.

19.title: Accumulate prefix sums
19.explanation: Walk the array while maintaining the running prefix sum and a set of sums seen before.

19.title: Detect a zero-sum slice
19.explanation: A prefix of zero gives a slice from the start; a repeated prefix gives a zero-sum slice between two positions. Return `0` only if neither occurs.

20.title: Create membership and visited state
20.explanation: Insert each number into a dictionary and mark it unvisited. Each sequence member will be consumed at most once.

20.title: Expand forward from an unvisited value
20.explanation: Skip values already consumed, then walk `num + 1`, `num + 2`, and so on while present, marking each visited and increasing the sequence length.

20.title: Expand backward and record the length
20.explanation: Walk downward from `num - 1` in the same way, then maximize the total count. The source returns negative infinity for an empty input.

21.title: Count every character
21.explanation: Build a frequency table for the characters. Palindrome feasibility depends only on how many frequencies are odd.

21.title: Allow at most one odd frequency
21.explanation: The first odd count can occupy the middle of an odd-length palindrome. A second odd count makes a rearranged palindrome impossible.

22.title: Count decimal digits
22.explanation: Repeated integer division by ten determines how many consecutive digit-window lengths must be examined.

22.title: Compute a window's digit product
22.explanation: Extract digits with `% 10`, multiply them, and return the product. In the captured helper, input zero incorrectly leaves the product as `1`.

22.title: Enumerate every consecutive digit window
22.explanation: For each width, isolate the current window with `% 10**i`, compute its product, and reject immediately if that product was seen before.

22.title: Shift to the next window
22.explanation: Store the new product, remove one trailing digit with `temp //= 10`, and repeat. Finishing all widths without a collision returns colorful.

23.title: Count the values in A
23.explanation: Build a frequency map so values can be emitted in the order requested by `B`, including duplicates.

23.title: Emit values named by B
23.explanation: Append each `B` value exactly as many times as it occurs in `A`, and remember which values have received priority ordering.

23.title: Sort only the leftover values
23.explanation: Collect values from `A` that never appeared in `B`, sort that remainder, and append it after the priority-ordered prefix.

24.title: Store all points for O(1) lookup
24.explanation: Put every `(x, y)` pair into a set so either missing corner of an axis-aligned rectangle can be tested directly.

24.title: Pair diagonal corners
24.explanation: For points with different x and y coordinates, check whether both opposite corners exist. Every rectangle is discovered twice, so divide the count by two.

25.title: Count points by x and y coordinate
25.explanation: Build independent frequency maps for each x coordinate and each y coordinate.

25.title: Count right angles at each point
25.explanation: At point `(x, y)`, choose any other point with x and any other point with y: `(xCount-1) * (yCount-1)`. Sum those choices over all vertices.

26.title: Count source-string characters
26.explanation: A frequency map captures how many copies of each character must be split among `A` identical substrings.

26.title: Check divisibility of every frequency
26.explanation: Each character count must be divisible by the replication count `A`. Any remainder makes equal substring replication impossible.

27.title: Normalize slopes with GCD
27.explanation: Use Euclid's algorithm so direction vectors can be reduced to a canonical integer slope instead of compared as floating-point numbers.

27.title: Choose an anchor and count overlaps
27.explanation: For each anchor point, reset its slope map. Identical points are counted separately in `overlap` because their direction vector is `(0, 0)`.

27.title: Reduce and count each direction
27.explanation: Subtract coordinates, divide by the GCD, and normalize signs so the same geometric line produces the same slope key.

27.title: Combine slope count with overlaps
27.explanation: The largest slope bucket plus the anchor and all overlapping points is the best line through this anchor; maximize it globally.

28.title: Build additive element hashes
28.explanation: Hash each array value as text and accumulate prefix sums. Equal hash sums are used as a proxy for equal sorted multisets.

28.title: Read both query ranges
28.explanation: For every query, extract the two inclusive subarray bounds before computing their prefix-hash sums.

28.title: Compare range hash sums
28.explanation: Subtract prefix hashes to obtain each range's additive hash, then append `1` on equality. Python's randomized hash and collisions make this probabilistic, not exact.

29.title: Count occurrences in A
29.explanation: Build a frequency table for the first array so duplicate common values can be capped correctly.

29.title: Intersect the two frequency maps
29.explanation: Count `B`, then for every value present in both arrays append it `min(countA, countB)` times.

30.title: Initialize KMP state
30.explanation: Reject unequal or empty strings, then allocate the LPS table for pattern `A`. `j` is the current matched-prefix length.

30.title: Build LPS and expose all rotations
30.explanation: KMP fallback fills `lps` in linear time. `B + B[:-1]` contains exactly the `N` possible cyclic-shift starting positions without duplicating rotation zero.

30.title: Count overlapping rotation matches
30.explanation: Run KMP over the doubled text. On a full match, increment the count and fall back through LPS so periodic strings can contribute overlapping matches.

31.title: Start with A's mandatory first character
31.explanation: The answer must contain a non-empty prefix of `A`, so initialize it with `A[0]`.

31.title: Extend A only while it helps
31.explanation: Append later characters of `A` while each is lexicographically smaller than `B[0]`, then append exactly the first character of `B`.

32.title: Compare mirrored characters
32.explanation: Move two pointers inward from the ends and permit one mismatched mirrored pair by setting `flag`.

32.title: Reject a second mismatch
32.explanation: If another unequal pair appears after `flag` is set, more than one replacement is needed and the answer is `NO`.

32.title: Handle the already-palindromic case
32.explanation: When no mismatch occurred, an even-length string cannot consume exactly one replacement without breaking symmetry; odd length can replace its center.

33.title: Form the palindrome-overlap pattern
33.explanation: The answer equals the unmatched prefix after overlapping `A` with its reverse. `findLPS` computes that overlap with KMP prefix-function state.

33.title: Build the LPS table
33.explanation: Advance both indices on a match; on mismatch, fall back to the previous border until a shorter prefix can continue, or write zero.

33.title: Read the longest palindromic prefix
33.explanation: Run LPS on `A + '@' + reverse(A)`. The final LPS value is the longest palindromic prefix, so the remaining suffix length is the number of front insertions.

34.title: Count occurrences of a
34.explanation: Only positions containing `'a'` matter, so count them in one scan.

34.title: Count substrings in the filtered sequence
34.explanation: For `c` occurrences, there are `c * (c + 1) / 2` non-empty contiguous choices in the sequence of those occurrences.

35.title: Handle the one-node list
35.explanation: Deleting the middle of a single-node list leaves an empty list, so return `None`.

35.title: Find and unlink the middle
35.explanation: Move `slow` one step and `fast` two steps while retaining `prev`. When `fast` ends, bypass `slow` with `prev.next = prev.next.next`.

36.title: Reverse exactly one K-node group
36.explanation: `reverse` rewires `n` links beginning at `head`, carrying `prev`, `curr`, and `temp` so no remainder of the list is lost.

36.title: Locate the next group boundary
36.explanation: `reverseFragment` walks at most `B` nodes to find where the current group ends and where the next group begins.

36.title: Reverse and reconnect recursively
36.explanation: Reverse the current group, attach its original head to the recursively processed remainder, and return the group's new head.

36.title: Process from the original head
36.explanation: The outer method starts recursive group reversal at `A` and returns the new head of the complete list.

37.title: Handle the one-node base case
37.explanation: A list with no second node is already reversed, so return its head unchanged.

37.title: Reverse links iteratively
37.explanation: Set the original head's next pointer to `None`, then repeatedly save `curr.next`, point `curr` backward to `prev`, and advance both pointers.

38.title: Initialize slow and fast pointers
38.explanation: Both pointers start at the head; `slow` will move one node for every two nodes traversed by `fast`.

38.title: Stop with slow at the middle
38.explanation: Continue while `fast` can take two steps. When it cannot, `slow` is the middle node (the second middle for even length), so return its value.

39.title: Handle an empty reversal range
39.explanation: When `B == C`, the selected segment contains one node and the list can be returned unchanged. Save the original head and numeric boundaries.

39.title: Find the left boundary
39.explanation: Traverse with a 1-based counter. At position `B`, save the node before the segment in `A` and the segment's original first node in `B`.

39.title: Reverse links through the right boundary
39.explanation: At position `C`, save the segment's new head and following node. For every position inside `[B, C]`, reverse the current link and advance using the saved next pointer.

39.title: Reconnect both sides
39.explanation: Attach the old segment head `B` to `D`. If reversal began at position one, return `C`; otherwise attach the left predecessor `A` to `C` and keep the original head.

40.title: Define node and list state
40.explanation: Each `Node` stores a value and next pointer; `LinkedList` stores only its head.

40.title: Insert at the head
40.explanation: Position `1` creates a new head and points it to the previous head. The captured method should return here but does not, which causes unnecessary traversal.

40.title: Walk to the insertion predecessor
40.explanation: Advance until `position - 1`, stopping if the list ends before that predecessor exists.

40.title: Splice in a middle or tail node
40.explanation: Reject an invalid predecessor; otherwise save its old successor, link the new node after the predecessor, then reconnect the saved successor.

40.title: Delete the head
40.explanation: For position `1`, advance `self.head` and return the removed head's value when the list is non-empty.

40.title: Walk to the deletion predecessor
40.explanation: Advance to the node immediately before the requested 1-based position, stopping when the list is too short.

40.title: Bypass the deleted node
40.explanation: If both predecessor and target exist, link around the target and return its value; invalid positions return nothing.

40.title: Print every node
40.explanation: Traverse from the head, printing spaces between values and a newline after the final value. Then create the shared list instance.

40.title: Expose the required function API
40.explanation: The global `insert_node`, `delete_node`, and `print_ll` functions delegate to the single shared `LinkedList` object expected by the judge.

41.title: Handle invalid and trivial inputs
41.explanation: Return `None` for no list and return the only node unchanged when its next pointer is absent.

41.title: Create a B-node lead
41.explanation: Advance `second` by `B` nodes while `first` stays at the head. If `second` becomes null exactly there, the node to remove is the head.

41.title: Move both pointers to the target
41.explanation: Advance both until `second` reaches the tail. `first.next` is then the B-th node from the end, so bypass it and return the head.

42.title: Start at the first sorted run
42.explanation: `curr` anchors the value to keep, while `temp` scans forward through nodes with the same value.

42.title: Link each run to the next distinct node
42.explanation: After skipping an equal-value run, set `curr.next` to the first different node and continue from there. Each distinct value keeps one node.

43.title: Handle one- and two-node loops
43.explanation: Break a self-loop directly. The next special case detects a two-node cycle returning to the head and severs its second link.

43.title: Detect a meeting inside the cycle
43.explanation: Move `slow` one step and `fast` two steps until they meet. Floyd's meeting proves a loop exists without extra storage.

43.title: Find the loop entry and its predecessor
43.explanation: Reset `slow` to the head and move both one step; `fast` reaches the entry while `prev` trails it at the final cycle node. Set `prev.next` to `None`.

44.title: Handle a one-node list
44.explanation: A single node already satisfies the reorder, so return it unchanged.

44.title: Store nodes and count half the list
44.explanation: Push every node onto a stack, then use half the stack length as the number of tail nodes that must be interleaved.

44.title: Interleave head and tail nodes
44.explanation: Pop the current tail, insert it after the current front node, then advance to the saved next front node. Finally terminate the list to remove stale links.

45.title: Establish merge-sort helpers
45.explanation: Return immediately for lists of length zero or one, then define an in-place merge for two already sorted linked lists.

45.title: Choose the merged head
45.explanation: Compare the first nodes of both lists, take the smaller as `head`, and advance only that source list.

45.title: Merge while both lists remain
45.explanation: Repeatedly attach the smaller current node to `temp`, advance that source, and move the merged tail forward.

45.title: Attach the remaining suffix
45.explanation: Once one source is exhausted, its competitor is already sorted, so attach that entire remainder and return the merged head.

45.title: Find the left-half tail
45.explanation: Start `fast` one node ahead so `slow` stops at the predecessor of the right half for both odd and even lengths.

45.title: Split, recurse, and merge
45.explanation: Cut the link after `mid`, recursively sort both independent halves, merge them, and invoke the recursive helper on the original head.

46.title: Define the reusable merge helper
46.explanation: If either list is empty, return the other. Otherwise prepare to merge by node value without allocating replacement nodes.

46.title: Choose the helper's head
46.explanation: Select the smaller first node as the merged head and advance the list that supplied it.

46.title: Merge the helper inputs
46.explanation: While both inputs remain, append the smaller current node and advance its source pointer.

46.title: Finish the helper and handle empty main inputs
46.explanation: Attach whichever helper input remains. The main implementation then applies the same empty-list base cases to `A` and `B`.

46.title: Choose the result head
46.explanation: Select the smaller of `A` and `B` as `head`, set `curr` to it, and advance the corresponding source.

46.title: Splice nodes in sorted order
46.explanation: Compare current nodes while both lists remain, attach the smaller one after `curr`, and advance both `curr` and that source.

46.title: Attach the last suffix
46.explanation: Link `curr.next` to whichever list is not empty. Its existing order is already correct, so no further comparisons are needed.

47.title: Scan from right with a decreasing stack
47.explanation: For each value from right to left, pop candidates `<= A[i]`; they can never be the next greater element for this or any earlier larger value.

47.title: Record the nearest surviving greater value
47.explanation: The stack top is the next greater element, or `-1` when none survives. Push the current value and reverse the accumulated answers back to input order.

48.title: Push operands and pop operand pairs
48.explanation: Numbers go onto the stack. On an operator, pop the right operand first and the left operand second; order matters for subtraction and division.

48.title: Evaluate and push each operation
48.explanation: Apply the token's operator, truncate division toward zero through `int(op2 / op1)`, and push the intermediate result. The final stack item is the expression value.

49.title: Maintain a decreasing candidate stack
49.explanation: Start with the first value. For each next value, pop every smaller-or-equal stack value and evaluate its XOR with the current value.

49.title: Compare the nearest larger neighbor
49.explanation: After popping, the stack top is the nearest surviving larger value; compare that XOR too, then push the current value. These are the only pairs that can maximize the required expression.

50.title: Set modulo arithmetic
50.explanation: Initialize the required modulus before computing boundary arrays and contribution totals.

50.title: Find previous smaller boundaries
50.explanation: Maintain increasing indices from left to right, popping strictly larger values. The surviving top is the previous `<=` boundary for each element.

50.title: Find previous greater boundaries
50.explanation: Maintain decreasing indices from left to right, popping strictly smaller values. The top becomes the previous `>=` boundary.

50.title: Find next smaller boundaries
50.explanation: Scan right to left and pop values `>= A[i]`. Using non-strict comparison on this side assigns duplicate minimum contributions exactly once.

50.title: Find next greater boundaries
50.explanation: Scan right to left and pop values `<= A[i]`. This is the duplicate-safe counterpart for maximum contributions.

50.title: Accumulate minimum contributions
50.explanation: For each index, count left and right choices before a smaller boundary. Their product is the number of subarrays where `A[i]` is the selected minimum.

50.title: Accumulate maxima and subtract minima
50.explanation: Repeat the contribution formula with greater boundaries, then return `(totalMax - totalMin)` normalized by the modulus.

51.title: Handle the one-bar histogram
51.explanation: A single bar's height is its full rectangle area; all longer histograms use nearest-smaller boundaries.

51.title: Build nearest-smaller indices
51.explanation: `nextSmaller` scans in a chosen direction with an increasing stack, popping heights `>=` the current bar so the top is strictly smaller.

51.title: Advance in the requested direction
51.explanation: Move left-to-right for `L` and right-to-left for `R`, then reverse right-scan results so both arrays align with original indices.

51.title: Compute both boundary arrays
51.explanation: `NSL` and `NSR` delimit how far every bar can extend while remaining the rectangle's minimum height.

51.title: Calculate widths with available boundaries
51.explanation: When both boundaries exist, width is `NSR - NSL - 1`; when neither exists, the bar spans the whole histogram. The one-sided case uses the existing boundary.

51.title: Handle an absent right boundary
51.explanation: If there is no smaller bar on the right, extend through the final index using `len(A) - NSL - 1`, then return the maximum area.

52.title: Remove unusable left candidates
52.explanation: Scan left to right with an increasing stack. Pop values `>= A[i]` because the answer must be strictly smaller.

52.title: Read and save the nearest smaller value
52.explanation: The surviving top is the nearest smaller element to the left; use `-1` when the stack is empty, then push the current value.

53.title: Represent valid passes as a stack
53.explanation: Keep the initial player `B` outside the stack and process each pass id in order.

53.title: Undo or record each pass
53.explanation: Id `0` cancels the previous pass by popping; any other id records a new holder. Return the initial player if every pass was canceled.

54.title: Initialize frequency-stack state
54.explanation: `freq` maps values to counts, `freqStack` groups values by current count, and `maxFreq` identifies the bucket to pop from.

54.title: Increase a pushed value's frequency
54.explanation: For push operations, increment `freq[x]` and raise `maxFreq` when this value reaches a new global frequency.

54.title: Push by frequency or pop the winning bucket
54.explanation: Append pushes to the stack for their new frequency, preserving recency. A pop removes the most recent value from the current `maxFreq` bucket.

54.title: Repair state after a pop
54.explanation: Delete an emptied top bucket and decrement `maxFreq`; decrease the popped value's count and append it to the output.

55.title: Move values through the auxiliary stack
55.explanation: Pop one value from `A`; while it is smaller than the auxiliary top, move larger values back to `A`, then insert it in order.

55.title: Restore displaced values and finish
55.explanation: Move qualifying values from `A` back onto the auxiliary stack before the next iteration. When `A` empties, the auxiliary stack contains the required sorted order.

56.title: Maintain data and minimum stacks
56.explanation: The main stack stores every value; `min_stack` stores each value that establishes or ties the current minimum.

56.title: Push while preserving the minimum
56.explanation: Push `x` to `min_stack` when it is `<=` the current minimum, then always push it to the data stack. Ties are retained so one pop does not lose the minimum.

56.title: Pop from both stacks when needed
56.explanation: Return nothing for an empty stack. Otherwise pop the data value and also pop `min_stack` when that value equals its top.

56.title: Read top and minimum in O(1)
56.explanation: `top` returns the latest data value and `getMin` returns the latest minimum, each using only the corresponding stack top or `-1` when empty.

57.title: Emit operands and open parentheses
57.explanation: Operands go directly to the postfix result. Opening parentheses are pushed as barriers between operator scopes.

57.title: Close groups and handle high precedence
57.explanation: A closing parenthesis pops operators until `(`. Exponentiation and multiplication/division pop operators of the precedence encoded by the source before being pushed.

57.title: Handle addition and subtraction
57.explanation: For low-precedence operators, flush every pending arithmetic operator above a parenthesis, then push the new operator.

57.title: Drain remaining operators
57.explanation: Any other character is appended as an operand. After the scan, pop all remaining operators to complete the postfix expression.

58.title: Push expression tokens
58.explanation: Scan the expression and push every token except `)`, preserving the contents of each parenthesized group.

58.title: Require an operator inside each group
58.explanation: On `)`, pop tokens until `(` and record whether an arithmetic operator appeared. No operator means the braces are redundant; otherwise remove `(` and continue.

59.title: Define sign composition
59.explanation: `evalSigns` returns plus when two signs agree and minus when they differ. This composes a term's local sign with the sign of its surrounding brackets.

59.title: Normalize the first term and scan
59.explanation: Add an explicit leading plus when needed, then walk the expression while maintaining whether each open bracket preserves or flips signs.

59.title: Apply signs through parentheses
59.explanation: On `+` or `-`, combine with the current bracket context before recording the variable term. Opening and closing parentheses push and pop that context.

59.title: Canonicalize and compare
59.explanation: Sort signed variables by name, evaluate both expressions into the same canonical form, and return whether the two normalized lists match.

60.title: Use a stack as the reduced string
60.explanation: Process characters left to right; the stack always represents the fully reduced prefix.

60.title: Cancel adjacent equal characters
60.explanation: If the current character equals the stack top, pop the pair; otherwise push it. Joining the final stack yields the stable reduced string.

61.title: Emit operands and open parentheses
61.explanation: Operands go directly to the postfix result. Opening parentheses are pushed as barriers between operator scopes.

61.title: Close groups and handle high precedence
61.explanation: A closing parenthesis pops operators until `(`. Exponentiation and multiplication/division pop operators according to the captured precedence rules.

61.title: Handle addition and subtraction
61.explanation: For low-precedence operators, flush every pending arithmetic operator above a parenthesis, then push the new operator.

61.title: Drain remaining operators
61.explanation: Append operands directly throughout the scan, then pop all remaining operators to complete the postfix expression.

62.title: Allocate vertical-height histograms
62.explanation: Create one height row per matrix row and copy the first binary row as the initial histogram.

62.title: Accumulate heights and test each row
62.explanation: A zero resets its column height; a one extends the height above it. Run largest-histogram-area on every completed row and keep the maximum.

62.title: Enter the histogram helper
62.explanation: Return the matrix-wide answer after all rows, while `largestRectangleArea` handles a single row and directly returns a one-bar case.

62.title: Build nearest-smaller indices
62.explanation: The local `nextSmaller` helper uses an increasing index stack and pops heights `>=` the current bar to find strict boundaries.

62.title: Complete directional scans
62.explanation: Move according to `L` or `R`; reverse the right-to-left result so every boundary aligns with the original histogram index.

62.title: Compute left and right boundaries
62.explanation: Call the helper in both directions. Those boundaries define the maximal width over which each bar remains the minimum height.

62.title: Calculate full and bounded widths
62.explanation: A bar with no smaller boundary spans the whole row; with both boundaries, its width is `NSR - NSL - 1`; one-sided cases use the existing edge.

62.title: Handle an open right edge
62.explanation: When the right boundary is absent, extend to the final column with `len(A) - NSL - 1`, then return the largest histogram area.
